weakness: The pipeline perceived the sphere once at t=0 and then executed an open-loop grasp; a sphere that started rolling at 4 cm/s was ~10 cm away by the time the fingers arrived, so every grasp closed on air.
how_found: Questioned A1 (the object stays where it was perceived). A sphere is the object most likely to move on its own, and the pipeline had no perception between the initial detection and the grasp.
why_missed: In the nominal task the sphere is always at rest, so a single (well-averaged) snapshot was enough and nothing in s0 rewarded re-checking. I averaged away perception noise but treated the scene as static, conflating 'precise' with 'current'.
fix: Estimate velocity from a time series of averaged detections (line fit, 1 s) before every attempt; if moving, go to a meeting point ahead on the path sized by speed x expected arm time, re-measure there (heading from the long baseline between the two measurements), lower the open fingers across the path, close when the object is predicted to reach the TCP mid-close; verify gripper_holding() and retry. Debugging also showed that re-orienting the wrist during the descent made the planner 5x slower, letting the object pass.
general_rule: Re-perceive an object immediately before every contact and estimate its velocity, not just its position; if it moves, plan to where it will be after your own motion time and verify the grasp before continuing.

weakness: Every motion was planned with no collision objects and the carry height was a constant (z=0.12), so a 15 cm wall between pick and place was hit by the arm and the held sphere. After obstacles were given to the planner, a second weakness appeared: the wrist yaw was fixed (45 deg), and with it the 20 cm-wide hand came within the planner's safety margin of the wall both at the pick and over the bin, so move_to was refused, and the pipeline ignored the refusal and closed the gripper on air.
how_found: Questioned A2 (the straight paths between waypoints are free). The pipeline never called get_obstacles() or used avoid, so any object between pick and place would be invisible to it.
why_missed: The nominal table is empty, so open-space screw motions always worked and the planner's collision checking was never exercised. I also treated the gripper as a point at the TCP and ignored the hand's footprint, which depends on the wrist yaw.
fix: Pass every non-task object to the planner on every motion; compute the carry height from the detected obstacle tops plus the held object's size (the planner does not model the object in the hand); move as lift, then horizontal transit, then descend. Try a ranked list of wrist yaws (diagonal to the bin first, then along the walls) at the pick and over the place, keeping the first one the planner accepts, and release slightly higher when the fingers are along the walls. Check every move_to return value before acting on it.
general_rule: Give the planner every known obstacle, inflate for the object you are carrying (which the planner does not see), treat the hand's footprint and orientation as free variables to search over, and check every motion's return value before the next action.

weakness: The round-2 fix computed one carry height as 'above the highest obstacle'. With a shelf over the bin, that height put the hand above the shelf, and every descent into the bin was blocked. Underneath it was a second weakness: the hand was always vertical (top-down), and a probe showed the arm cannot reach any point under a 30 cm overhang with a vertical hand, even with the shelf removed from the planner. A forward tilt of 0.6-0.9 rad reaches all of them.
how_found: Questioned B4 (obstacles only matter by their top). The carry height was derived from max(top) alone, which treats every obstacle as a floor and never as a ceiling.
why_missed: The round-2 obstacle was a wall, and for a wall 'go higher' is always correct, so the fix generalised the instance instead of the geometry. The vertical hand had never been questioned because every earlier target was in open space.
fix: Candidate carry heights are the lowest safe height plus each obstacle top + clearance. A height is kept only if the held object clears every obstacle over the pick-place corridor in z, from both below and above. Heights are tried lowest first, and at each height the pipeline searches hand tilt (0, 0.6, 0.9 rad forward) x wrist yaw, taking the first transfer and descent the planner accepts. It releases slightly higher when the hand is tilted or the fingers are along the walls.
general_rule: Free space is bounded from above as well as below: choose the lowest motion that keeps the carried object clear in every direction, and when a target is unreachable, search the hand's full orientation (tilt as well as yaw) before concluding it is blocked.

weakness: The grasp height was a constant (sphere radius above z=0, i.e. 'the object rests on the table'), while x and y came from perception. With the sphere on a 12 cm platform, the pre-grasp pose was inside the platform and the grasp pose 12 cm below the sphere. The planner refused every one of them, and the pipeline retried the same impossible poses until it gave up.
how_found: Questioned B5. The pipeline used the measured x and y of the object but threw away the measured z in favour of a constant that encoded a belief about the support surface.
why_missed: On the nominal task the constant and the measurement agree to the millimetre, so the shortcut looked harmless; it was written when 'the table' was the only support surface in the scene. Earlier fixes re-measured position for motion (x, y, velocity) but never audited which coordinates were still hard-coded.
fix: All grasp and pre-grasp heights now come from the averaged measured position of the object (static and rolling grasps). The existing carry-height logic then treats the platform as an obstacle under the corridor and lifts the sphere above it.
general_rule: Derive every coordinate of a target pose from perception; any constant that encodes where an object 'normally' is (support height, orientation, size) is an untested assumption that will fail the first time the object is somewhere else.

weakness: The pipeline handled every non-task object only as an obstacle to plan around. With a block already sitting in the bin, it scored 0.0 (gate). The failing episodes were not traced; the inferred mechanism is that the block, given to the planner as an obstacle, made every descent into the bin collide, and the pipeline has no action that frees the goal.
how_found: Questioned C1 (the goal is empty). Every fix so far had made the pipeline better at avoiding things, which made it more likely to treat a blocked goal as unreachable rather than as something to change.
why_missed: The nominal bin is always empty, and the obstacle fixes of rounds 2-3 framed every other object as fixed scenery. I never asked whether the precondition of the final action (an empty target) actually held.
fix: Before picking up the sphere (while the hand is still empty), detect any non-task object inside the goal footprint, grasp it (excluding it from the planner's obstacle list for that grasp), move it to free table space beside the goal on the side away from the sphere, re-check the goal, and only then re-measure the obstacles and run the normal pick-and-place.
general_rule: Before an action, check its preconditions on the target (free, reachable, stable), and when one fails, consider changing the scene (move the blocker, while the hand is free) instead of only planning around it.
